query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment that forms a uniform spinel-like oxide layer on the CoCrFeNi surface will stabilize the frictional and wear behavior over the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy matrix exhibiting native, non-uniform oxide formation and grain structures that lead to inconsistent tribological performance across temperatures.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment at approximately 700–750 °C in a low oxygen partial pressure environment (around 10⁻³ to 10⁻² atm) to deliberately form an adherent, self-lubricating spinel-like oxide layer on the surface.
generation.conditions: Sliding wear tests performed under normal loads of approximately 10–30 N in a dry or mild humidity environment, with the operational temperature spanning from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: The pre-formed, coherent oxide layer (e.g., spinel-like structure) acting as a protective, self-lubricating tribo-layer.
generation.mechanism: The oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact, lowers adhesive and abrasive interactions during sliding, and provides consistent lubrication by maintaining its integrity across the wide temperature range. This pre-formed film minimizes unexpected oxidation kinetics that occur during wear, thus stabilizing friction and wear responses from RT to high temperatures.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated CoCrFeNi matrix, the pre-oxidized alloy is expected to exhibit a lower and more stable coefficient of friction as well as a reduced specific wear rate across the entire temperature regime.
generation.baseline: Untreated CoCrFeNi samples that rely on in situ tribo-oxidation, which leads to inconsistent oxide layer formation and fluctuating friction and wear performance, especially at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: Valid under sliding conditions with normal loads of 10–30 N in dry or mildly humid environments and within the temperature range from room temperature up to 800 °C.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the long-term cyclic stability of the pre-formed oxide layer and its resistance to mechanical degradation under continuous sliding, particularly near the upper temperature limit.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of CoCrFeNi samples: one group subjected to the controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment (700–750 °C in 10⁻³–10⁻² atm O₂) and the other left untreated. Conduct sliding wear tests over the entire temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under normal loads of 10–30 N in a controlled dry/mild humidity environment. Monitor and record the friction coefficients and wear rates along with surface oxide layer integrity using SEM and EDS analysis.
measurements: Coefficient of friction across temperature range
Morphological and compositional analysis (SEM/EDS) of the oxide layer before and after tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples do not show a statistically significant reduction in friction coefficient and wear rate compared to untreated samples across the temperature range, or if the oxide layer degrades rapidly during sliding (demonstrated by loss of uniformity or coherence), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Thus, if cooperative heterostructures capable of releasing frictional stress in stages are configured in the alloy, it is expected to suppress the sliding-induced deformation. In contrast, upon wear at high temperatures (≥600 °C), the wear behavior of the material becomes quite complex, stemming from the prevalence of surface adhesion and tribo-oxidation at the friction interface [,]. High-temperature sliding tends to soften the metallic surface that endows the near-surface material susceptible to chemical instability caused by counterbody materials or environmental oxygen, triggering severe delamination wear and composition segregation at the friction interface that exacerbates wear [,]. Materials become more dependent on tribochemical protection upon high-temperature wear due to deterioration in stiffness [,]. Tribo-oxidation may promote the formation of a protective oxide layer (glaze layer) consisting of various nanocrystalline (NC) oxides on the worn surface, which assists in enhancing the friction interface while providing solid lubrication [,,]. AbstractThe effect and mechanism of grain sizes on the tribological behavior of CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy (HEA) were studied by friction experiments and wear morphology analysis. Under normal low load and low sliding speed, the primary wear mechanism of the HEA samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the samples are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. The oxide layer formed under the action of friction heat of the coarse grain (CG) sample is easy to break due to the softening of the CG. With the increase of normal load and sliding speed, the wear mechanisms of the HEA samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation. The oxide layer of CG sample has many cracks, and the worn surface also has plastic deformation, which leads to the increase of friction coefficient and specific wear rate and the decrease of wear resistance. Therefore, the fine grain size HEA sample has better wear resistance than the CG sample due to its high surface strength.Keywords: high entropy alloy, grain size, tribological behavior, wear mechanism

In the present study, the tribological properties of different grain sizes CoCrFeMnNi HEAs were systematically analyzed based on sliding experiments and worn surface morphology characterization under different sliding speeds and normal loads. The results can be summarized as follows: Under the normal low load and low sliding speed, the main wear mechanism of FG and CG samples is adhesive wear. With the increase in sliding speed, the wear mechanisms are adhesive wear and oxidation wear. However, the material of CG is easy to soften under the action of friction heat during high sliding speed, and the oxide layer formed is easy to fracture. Under the normal high load, the wear mechanisms of FG and CG samples are mainly adhesive wear, oxidation wear, and plastic deformation with the increase of sliding speed. The oxidation layer formed on CG sample has many cracks, and the wear surface of CG sample also has plastic deformation, resulting in an increase in friction coefficient and specific wear rate and a decrease in wear resistance. Therefore, under high load and low load, FG sample has good wear resistance due to its high surface strength.

decision.trend: Early work on CoCrFeNi-type systems introduced oxide particles (e.g., Y2O3) to improve wear resistance, but room-temperature friction did not markedly change. Subsequent studies showed that refining near-surface grains via severe sliding could yield ultra-nanocrystalline layers and low friction in vacuum for a similar (CoCrFeMnNi) alloy, yet coverage of all service temperatures was incomplete. Other researchers tackled wide-range wear stability (up to 800 °C) by engineering multi-scale or composite surfaces capable of forming self-protecting tribo-layers. Meanwhile, plasma-sprayed CoCrFeNi-based coatings validated that dense, well-bonded lamellae can reduce wear at intermediate temperatures. However, a robust method to ensure stable, low-friction operation across the entire 25 °C to 800 °C span in a simple CoCrFeNi matrix remains elusive.
decision.unsolved: A single-step approach that consistently stabilizes friction and low wear from ambient to 800 °C—without resorting to major chemical additions—has not been demonstrated. Conventional coatings can degrade or oxidize inconsistently at high temperature, while purely bulk microstructure modifications typically falter at one end of the temperature spectrum or the other.
decision.lever: Apply a controlled pre-oxidation heat treatment in low oxygen partial pressure to create a stable, self-lubricating spinel-like oxide on the CoCrFeNi surface. Temperature: ~700–750 °C; partial pressure O2 ~10^-3–10^-2 atm; normal loads ~10–30 N; environment: dry or mild humidity. This adherent oxide film is hypothesized to minimize adhesive and abrasive wear from room temperature up to 800 °C by forming a protective tribo-layer that remains stable under sliding.
decision.why: Prior work shows oxide dispersions can improve wear and hardness, and self-sustaining tribo-oxide films can reduce friction across wide temperature ranges. By deliberately growing a robust oxide layer before service, the alloy can transition between low to high temperatures without suffering from excessive wear or friction spikes, leveraging the protective nature of the oxide throughout the entire sliding regime.
